flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
Of course. I think our initial response is always to acknowledge how they feel. I think as a child, that's truly all you want to be heard. And the littlest things may seem like a really big deal. And at the moment, it is a big deal for them. So acknowledging how they feel always. We practice a lot with being at their level. We always work at their level. And I think that helps a lot with understanding and helping them understand that I'm right here with you and I hear you. And I know it's tough. She took your toy, but we can work through that and we don't have to throw our bodies and teaching them the skills that they're just learning at, you know, our center starts at 12 months. So even then. And then the communication, it's still growing. Their language skills, their fine motor, their gross motor skills are still growing. So I think just being there with them, for one, acknowledging their feelings and then assessing the situation. Can we redirect the conflict? Can we resolve the conflict? Is it a moment where we can learn to share? Is it a moment where you learn to, you know, base a boundary that you don't want to share right now and we learn to communicate that? So I think communication. So one, always acknowledging them and then showing them that there's other ways.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time you felt overwhelmed at work with children present. What did you do to manage yourself?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q4 Attempt 1]
We have a one to four ratio, but even then we have a classroom of 18 children and we are about eight to nine staff in our classroom itself. So I think teamwork plays a really big role. If I ever do feel stressed, I think it's a moment of never feeling the need to keep it all to myself because we do believe in teamwork. And hey, do you think you can assess me with this? Or my master teacher does a really great job at being very open. Like if you cannot handle a situation or you do not know how, I'm always here to talk you through it. I'm always here to show you the steps that we can take. Most of the time I do think that some children, depending on where we are with their skill sets, it's not only difficult to teach them that when you're learning it yourself sometimes, but I think it's very important to just meet them where they are. And you have to remind yourself that as well. And I don't think this field is for the faint heart. I think you have to have a really open mind on that and to know what you're stepping into because there is no language and we are learning it, you know. So I think a stressful situation calls for a lot of teamwork.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Imagine you’re caring for a child who clearly does not want to be touched during a routine task, like diapering, helping with clothing, or guiding them physically. They are pulling away or saying no. Walk me through exactly what you would do, step by step
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q5 Attempt 1]
I want to say, for one, redirecting is practiced a lot. I'm going to help you if you need help. But if they're pulling away, there is moments where you just have to give the child space and, okay, I can wait with you and for you until you're ready. And most of the time when you give them space and you just give them that understanding, at some point they are ready to work with you. And I think the more you push or the more you really try to, you know, assess the situation when they don't want assessing can overstimulate or maybe agitate them. So most of the time we do give space.
